title: Cornell Faces Pressure for Broader Reform After Faculty No-Confidence Vote
author: Rebecca Schneid; Connor Greene
body:
After weeks of pressure on Cornell University’s administration over its handling of an alleged gang rape by fraternity members, the Faculty Senate passed a resolution of no confidence on Nov. 6. The vote of 75–50, with five abstentions, signaled a deepening rift over the university’s leadership and its ability to “effectively address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault at Cornell University.”

The resolution, which is one sentence long, does not recommend any removals, have any official recommendations for the administration, or impact whether university President Michael Kotlikoff remains in his role.

It serves as a formal rebuke and gesture of solidarity after a former student, Jane Doe, filed a lawsuit Sept. 16 claiming she was raped at a fraternity house at Cornell in 2024. The lawsuit also accuses Cornell of violating New York law.

In response to the vote, Chair Anne Meinig Smalling said that the Board of Trustees “remains confident that President Kotlikoff and his administration are the right leaders to thoughtfully and comprehensively address the serious problem of sexual assault on our campus.”

She pointed to measures that were announced Oct. 13 by the university as a means to “strengthen campus safety”—one of which involved banning Interfraternity Council (IFC) houses from hosting parties or social events for the rest of the academic year. Other measures included adding staff to Cornell’s Office of Civil Rights, working with New York State Police to utilize trauma-informed criminal investigators, and improving education regarding the bystander effect.

“These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now,” Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff said in the Oct. 13 announcement.

Students and faculty expressed frustration when the measures were first announced.

Jack Huber, a member of Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), told TIME the following day that the outlined measures were “not nearly enough to tackle this issue on an institutional level.”

To take the efforts further, he explained, students are calling on the university to revoke the degrees of the accused fraternity members; establish independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault; and commission an external review of the school’s handling of the case.

Cornell acknowledged in its October statement that the school has “fallen short” and pointed to the independent review that was launched by the university’s Board of Trustees. It is being led by former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates.

Separately, New York Attorney General Letitia James appointed former federal prosecutor Jacqueline Kelly on Nov. 4 to lead the criminal investigation into the alleged assault. Kelly’s team will review previous investigative records, gather evidence and interview witnesses, reporting to the attorney general’s office.

Huber said that the campus community believes Cornell is ultimately deflecting responsibility.

“The vast majority of campus is absolutely not satisfied by this response, and many of which are enraged that the administration would so blatantly redirect blame away from themselves to get Cornell out of the news,” he explained.

The school said on Sept. 28 that when Doe reported the alleged assault in late 2024, it acted in accordance with federal law and triggered Title IX proceedings. An investigation took place in early 2025.

“After investigation, and pursuant to federal law, the matter was sent to a hearing where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days,” the school’s statement said, noting that it ultimately applied a “range of sanctions” to the accused students, including expulsions and suspensions.

“The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence,” it continued.

The statement also pointed out that Cornell’s Chi Phi chapter was closed in 2024 and remained barred from campus.

Kotlikoff’s office did not reply to TIME’s request for comment.

Sabrina Karim, a government professor at Cornell, told TIME in October that she views the fraternity events ban as a “testing ground for a different policy going forward,” and a move that will buy time to evaluate what’s next.

She agreed that the ban does not go far enough—explaining that a broader and more coordinated approach may be necessary, especially in a rural environment like Ithaca, New York.

Cornell is located in a rural pocket of the Finger Lakes region in upstate New York, surrounded by hills and country roads. Karim said that the climate requires a more robust effort by the university to connect students with external resources, like law enforcement.

“There needs to be, just, a better system,” she said.

As an update to the Oct. 13 measures, Cornell announced Oct. 29 that it had finalized an agreement allowing survivors pursuing criminal charges to choose whether New York State Police or Cornell University Police investigates their case. The arrangement will remain in place throughout the independent review led by Yates. The school did not mention coordinated efforts that might take place beyond that timeline.

Cornell faces calls for sexual assault reform

Professor Paul Ortiz introduced the no-confidence resolution Oct. 7. In a news conference after the vote last week, Ortiz told the press that he and other faculty had heard “from scores of current students, alumni, staff and faculty that the Jane Doe case was the tip of the iceberg.”

“For years and even generations, hundreds of Cornell students and employees have endured rape and sexual assault, only to have their experiences and traumas ignored and swept under the rug by this and previous administrations,” Ortiz added.

At the Nov. 6 press conference, Ortiz also announced plans for a project to collect accounts from survivors of sexual misconduct in the Cornell community and Ithaca.

Speaking with TIME last month, soon after the resolution was first introduced, professors at Cornell said that many faculty members distrust the administration.

Risa Lieberwitz, a professor in the School of Industrial and Labor Relations, said last month that Cornell’s administration does not adequately listen to campus governance bodies such as the Faculty Senate, student assemblies, and unions.

She said it has taken a “top down” approach to decision-making and “has not shown respect or real commitment to democratic campus governance.”

Others believed that the school’s ban on fraternity events was more of a response to external pressure than a push for long-lasting cultural change on campus.

Julia Chang, a professor of Hispanic studies at Cornell, said the timing felt “very suspicious,” since it came as the Faculty Senate considered its no-confidence resolution.

“Trust is eroded between faculty and administration, and between students and administration,” Chang told TIME in October. “We see this administration as one that is reacting to the news, and to the bad PR, as opposed to leading on this issue.”

“I continue to have concerns, and I know many of my colleagues continue to have concerns, that the Cornell administration is reactive,” Lieberwitz said. “It is reacting to pressure on it in a very drip, drip, drip way.”

In light of that perception, student organizers believe that the only way to get the changes they’re seeking is by continuing to apply pressure.

“What's clear to us is that the administration is trying to scapegoat fraternities instead of making any commitment to institutional change—change in line with the demands that SDC and dozens of other organizations put forward,” Huber said. “And the fact that it is only a year shows that they are really using this as a temporary fix, something to get the administration out of the news cycle.”

SDC is one of the many student groups that organized a “Justice for Survivors” rally on Oct. 5. Thousands of students and community members attended the protest, according to the Cornell Sun. The SDC also co-sponsored a seven-hour sit-in organized by the school’s NAACP and Black Students United groups on Oct. 7.

On Oct. 16, student activist organization groups on campus held a mock trial of the lawsuit defendants outside a Cornell Board of Trustees meeting. They “tried” several administrators, including Kotlikoff. According to the Sun, nearly 50 students took turns smashing and stabbing photographs of the seven fraternity brothers named in Doe’s lawsuit.

“We are still putting pressure on the administration and we are not going to stop until we get our demands,” Huber said. “We will not be satisfied until we have institutional change and an independent judicial system, so something like this can never be covered up again.”
